decks.title: Accounting Equation, Double Entry and Classification of Accounts
goals: State the accounting equation and show the effect of a series of transactions on assets, liabilities and capital
Find a missing element of the equation, and the profit of a year from the change in capital
Classify accounts as personal, real or nominal and as assets, liabilities, capital, incomes or expenses, and apply the rules of debit and credit

slides.heading: The accounting equation and the double entry system
slides.body_md: Part 1: how every transaction keeps the books in balance.

rows: What the firm owns: cash, stock, debtors, furniture
What it owes outsiders: creditors, loans
What the owner has put in and left in

visual.alt: Table showing the accounting equation: assets equal liabilities plus capital, with what each term covers

slides.narration: Welcome to Chapter three of Class eleven accounts. Every business owns resources and owes claims against them. This part shows how the resources, the liabilities and the owner capital always stay in balance, how each transaction changes them, and how accounts are classified so that we know which side to debit and which to credit.

slides.heading: What the accounting equation says

rows: The resources of a firm are always equal to the claims against them
Every transaction has two aspects of equal value
Find the owner's capital when assets and liabilities are known
Test that the position is in balance after each transaction
Records only what can be stated in money and does not show profit as such

visual.alt: Table on the accounting equation: meaning, why it holds, two uses and a limit

slides.narration: The accounting equation says that the resources of a firm always equal the claims against them. It holds because every transaction has two aspects of equal value. The owner can use it to find capital when assets and liabilities are known, and to test that the position stays in balance. Its limit is that it records only what can be stated in money.

slides.heading: Assets, liabilities and capital

rows: Resources owned that have value to the firm
Amounts the firm owes to outsiders
The owner's claim: investment plus profit less drawings
Cash brought in by the proprietor

visual.alt: Table defining assets, liabilities and capital with examples

slides.narration: Assets are resources the firm owns, such as cash, stock, debtors and machinery. Liabilities are amounts it owes to outsiders, such as creditors and a bank loan. Capital is the claim of the owner, which is what the owner has put in plus profit left in, less drawings. Together the liabilities and the capital are the claims against the assets.

slides.heading: Three forms of the equation

rows: Checks the position after a transaction

visual.alt: Table of the three forms of the accounting equation and what each finds

slides.narration: The same equation can be written in three ways. Assets equal liabilities plus capital is used to check the position after a transaction. Capital equals assets less liabilities finds the owner capital. Liabilities equal assets less capital finds what the firm owes outsiders. Whichever element is missing, the other two give it.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: eight transactions of Tezpur Tea Stall
slides.body_md: **Tezpur Tea Stall**, an imagined firm. After every step, assets equal liabilities plus capital.
bullets: A sale above cost raises cash and capital by the profit (₹8,000 on the cash sale).
Drawings and rent lower cash and capital.
At the end: assets ₹1,85,500 = creditors ₹10,000 + capital ₹1,75,500.

rows: Owner starts with cash ₹1,50,000 and furniture ₹30,000
Sold goods costing ₹12,000 on credit for ₹14,500

visual.alt: Equation table for Tezpur Tea Stall: eight transactions, ending with cash 1,18,000, stock 23,000, debtors 14,500, furniture 30,000, creditors 10,000 and capital 1,75,500 rupees

slides.narration: Tezpur Tea Stall starts with cash of rupees one lakh fifty thousand and furniture of rupees thirty thousand, so capital is rupees one lakh eighty thousand. Buying goods for cash swaps assets. Buying on credit raises stock and creditors. Each sale above cost raises capital by the profit. Drawings and rent lower capital. At the end, assets of rupees one lakh eighty five thousand five hundred equal creditors of rupees ten thousand plus capital of rupees one lakh seventy five thousand five hundred.

slides.heading: How five kinds of transaction act on the equation

rows: Rent paid; goods taken by the owner

visual.alt: Table of five kinds of transaction and their effect on assets, liabilities and capital

slides.narration: Transactions fall into five patterns. A swap of assets changes neither side. A credit purchase raises an asset and a liability. Paying a liability lowers an asset and the liability. Profit, income or fresh capital raises an asset and capital. Drawings, expenses and losses lower an asset and capital. Name the pattern first, and the effect on the equation follows.

slides.heading: Quick check: find the capital
slides.body_md: A firm has assets of ₹6,15,000 and outside liabilities of ₹2,40,000.
slides.narration: Use the second form of the equation. Capital is found by taking the liabilities away from the assets. Work out the figure and enter it in rupees.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: finding the missing element
slides.body_md: In each case one element is missing; the other two give it by the equation.

visual.alt: Table of three cases in which one element of the accounting equation is found from the other two

slides.narration: In case A the assets are rupees six lakh forty thousand and the liabilities are rupees two lakh ten thousand, so capital is rupees four lakh thirty thousand. In case B liabilities and capital together make assets of rupees five lakh. In case C, taking capital from assets leaves liabilities of rupees one lakh twenty thousand. Always rewrite the equation to isolate the missing element.

slides.heading: Profit from the change in capital
slides.body_md: If the books record no profit directly, profit is the change in capital, corrected for drawings and fresh capital.

visual.alt: Table finding profit from capital: closing 5,05,000 less opening 4,30,000 plus drawings 36,000 less fresh capital 20,000 gives profit 91,000 rupees

slides.narration: Capital grows by profit and by fresh capital, and falls by drawings. So profit equals closing capital, less opening capital, plus drawings, less fresh capital. Here the closing capital is rupees five lakh five thousand and the opening capital is rupees four lakh thirty thousand. After adding the drawings and removing the fresh capital, the profit for the year is rupees ninety one thousand.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: Ongole Bakery, a loan and a sale at a profit
slides.body_md: **Ongole Bakery**, an imagined firm, starts with capital ₹2,20,000.
bullets: A bank loan raises cash and a liability together.
Goods costing ₹18,000 sold on credit for ₹23,000: capital rises by ₹5,000.
Goods taken by the owner reduce stock and capital by ₹7,000.

rows: Took a bank loan ₹50,000 into cash
Owner took goods costing ₹7,000 for personal use
Sold goods costing ₹18,000 on credit for ₹23,000

visual.alt: Equation table for Ongole Bakery: starting capital 2,20,000 and seven transactions, ending with assets 3,05,000 and capital 2,15,000 rupees

slides.narration: Ongole Bakery starts with capital of rupees two lakh twenty thousand. A bank loan of rupees fifty thousand raises cash and a liability. Commission raises capital, and wages lower it. Goods taken by the owner lower stock and capital. A credit sale above cost raises debtors and capital. At the end, assets of rupees three lakh five thousand equal the liabilities and the capital of rupees two lakh fifteen thousand.

slides.heading: Double entry: two accounts, equal amounts
slides.body_md: Every transaction has a **debit** aspect and a **credit** aspect of equal value, so the total debits always equal the total credits.

nodes.label: A transaction occurs
Two accounts are affected
One account is debited, another credited
Equal amounts: debits equal credits

visual.alt: Flow: a transaction affects two accounts, one is debited and one credited, in equal amounts

slides.narration: The double entry system records both aspects of every transaction. One account is debited and another is credited, always for equal amounts. This is the accounting equation in action. Since the two sides are equal, total debits equal total credits, and any difference points to an error somewhere in the books.

slides.heading: Two ways of classifying accounts

rows: Personal (natural, artificial, representative), real (tangible, intangible), nominal
Assets, liabilities, capital, revenues or incomes, expenses or losses

visual.alt: Table of the traditional and modern classification of accounts

slides.narration: Accounts can be classified in two ways. The traditional way has personal accounts, which may be natural, artificial or representative, real accounts, and nominal accounts. The modern way groups accounts as assets, liabilities, capital, revenues or incomes, and expenses or losses. Both lead to the same debit and credit, so a student should know both.

slides.heading: Personal accounts

rows: Rao Brothers A/c, Meena Kapoor A/c
A body the law treats as a person
A bank, a club, a company
A person or persons through an item
Outstanding Rent A/c, Prepaid Insurance A/c

visual.alt: Table of natural, artificial and representative personal accounts with examples

slides.narration: A personal account relates to a person. A natural personal account is that of a living person, such as a debtor or a creditor. An artificial personal account is that of a body the law treats as a person, such as a bank or a company. A representative personal account stands for persons through an item, such as outstanding rent or prepaid insurance.

slides.heading: Real and nominal accounts

rows: Things owned that can be touched
Cash A/c, Machinery A/c, Furniture A/c
Things owned with no physical form
Salaries A/c, Bad Debts A/c, Interest Received A/c

visual.alt: Table of real and nominal accounts with examples

slides.narration: A real account relates to things the firm owns. Tangible ones can be touched, such as cash, machinery and furniture. Intangible ones have no physical form, such as goodwill and patents. A nominal account relates to expenses, losses, incomes and gains, such as salaries, bad debts and interest received. Nominal accounts are closed at the end of the year.

slides.heading: Quick check: which kind of account?
slides.body_md: A firm records the right to use a patented design in a Patents account.
slides.narration: Ask whether the item is owned by the firm, whether it stands for a person, and whether it is an expense or a loss. Then choose the class that fits.

slides.heading: The modern classification and its rules

visual.alt: Table of the five modern classes of accounts and the side on which each increases and decreases

slides.narration: In the modern classification an asset or an expense increases on the debit side and decreases on the credit side. A liability, the capital and a revenue increase on the credit side and decrease on the debit side. The side of increase is the one to remember, and the opposite side serves for a decrease. Drawings, which reduce capital, are debited.

slides.heading: The traditional rules of debit and credit

visual.alt: Table of the traditional rules of debit and credit for personal, real and nominal accounts

slides.narration: In the traditional system the rule depends on the class. For a personal account, debit the receiver and credit the giver. For a real account, debit what comes in and credit what goes out. For a nominal account, debit all expenses and losses and credit all incomes and gains. Apply the rule to each account in the transaction, and one debit and one credit emerge.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: analysing six transactions
slides.body_md: For each imagined transaction, name the two accounts, their classes, and the debit and the credit.
bullets: Machinery bought for cash: Machinery up (debit), Cash down (credit).
Rent due, not paid: Rent up (debit), Outstanding Rent up (credit).
A creditor paid: Rao Brothers down (debit), Cash down (credit).

rows: Took a loan from Vindhya Bank into cash
Loan from Vindhya Bank A/c (Personal (artificial); Liability)
Paid Rao Brothers, a creditor, in cash
Rent of the month is due but not yet paid
Owner brought more cash into the business

visual.alt: Analysis table of six imagined transactions: the accounts debited and credited, each with its traditional and modern class

slides.narration: Take six transactions. Machinery bought for cash debits machinery and credits cash. Salaries paid debit salaries and credit cash. A bank loan taken in cash debits cash and credits the loan. Paying a creditor debits the creditor and credits cash. Rent due but unpaid debits rent and credits outstanding rent. More capital brought in debits cash and credits capital.

slides.heading: Quick check: repaying a loan
slides.body_md: A firm repays part of its bank loan in cash.
slides.narration: A loan is a liability. Think about what happens to the loan when part of it is repaid, and on which side a fall in a liability is shown.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: Assets = Liabilities + Capital after every transaction.
Five patterns of effect; profit raises capital, drawings lower it.
Double entry: equal debits and credits.
Classify as personal, real or nominal, and as assets, liabilities, capital, incomes or expenses.

rows: Assets = Liabilities + Capital after every transaction
Swap, credit purchase, payment, profit or capital, drawings or expense
Two accounts, equal debit and credit
Personal, real, nominal; assets, liabilities, capital, incomes, expenses
Debit the receiver, what comes in, expenses; credit the giver, what goes out, incomes

visual.alt: Summary table of the accounting equation, effects of transactions, double entry, classification and rules

slides.narration: To sum up. The accounting equation holds after every transaction. Transactions follow five patterns. Double entry records two aspects in equal amounts. Accounts are classified in the traditional way and in the modern way, and each class has a rule that tells us which side to debit and which to credit. The next part turns these rules into journal entries.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Show the equation after each step in a table.
Name the class of every account you debit or credit.
Check the profit by the change in capital.

rows: Show the equation after each step
Step marks go to each correct row
Name the class of each account
Marks go to reasoning as well as the answer
Check that the two sides are equal

visual.alt: Exam tips table for the accounting equation and the classification of accounts

slides.narration: In the examination, show the equation in a table after each step, so that every correct row earns a mark. Name the class of each account you use, because the reasoning is rewarded as well as the answer. When finding profit from capital, include drawings and fresh capital, and check that both sides of the equation agree.

decks.title: The Journal and Goods and Services Tax (Theory)
goals: Explain the meaning, format and advantages of the journal and write simple, compound and opening entries with narrations
Journalise discounts, returns, drawings, goods lost or given as charity, bad debts, depreciation, interest and outstanding or prepaid items
Explain in outline what Goods and Services Tax is, its three components and input tax credit

slides.heading: The journal: where every transaction is first recorded
slides.body_md: Part 2: from a transaction to a journal entry, and a theoretical look at GST.

visual.alt: Table showing the ruling of a journal with its five columns and one entry with a narration

slides.narration: Welcome to the second part of Chapter three. Having learned how accounts are classified and which side to debit or credit, we now record transactions in the journal. We write simple, compound and opening entries with narrations, and then take a short, theoretical look at goods and services tax.

slides.heading: Where the journal fits
slides.body_md: The journal is the **book of original entry**: each transaction is recorded in it first, in date order.

nodes.label: Source document
Journal: the book of original entry
Ledger: posting
Trial balance
Final accounts

visual.alt: Flow: from the source document to the journal, then the ledger, the trial balance and the final accounts

slides.narration: Every transaction begins with a source document, such as a bill or a voucher. It is recorded first in the journal, which is why the journal is called the book of original entry. From the journal the entries are posted to the ledger, which is the subject of the next chapter, and then come the trial balance and the final accounts.

slides.heading: Advantages of the journal

rows: Every transaction is traced from one place
The debit and credit of an entry are seen side by side
The reason for the entry is stated for later reference
Supports checking and auditing of the accounts

visual.alt: Table of five advantages of the journal

slides.narration: The journal gives a record in the order of dates, so any transaction can be traced from one place. It shows the debit and the credit of each entry side by side, and the narration gives the reason. Errors can be checked before posting, and the book is useful as evidence when the accounts are checked or audited.

slides.heading: Passing an entry in five steps

nodes.label: Find the accounts affected
Classify each account
Apply the rule of debit and credit
Write debit first, credit after "To"
Add the narration

visual.alt: Flow of five steps for passing a journal entry

slides.narration: To pass an entry, first find the two or more accounts affected. Next classify each one. Then apply the rule of debit and credit. Write the account to be debited first, with the abbreviation for debit, and write the account to be credited on the next line, indented, after the word To. Finally write the narration, beginning with the word Being.

slides.heading: Quick check: do the totals agree?
slides.body_md: A firm sells goods partly for cash and partly on credit in a single entry.
slides.narration: Think about whether a compound entry follows the same rule as a simple entry. What must be true of the debit side and the credit side of every entry?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: purchases, sales and returns
slides.body_md: **Kolar Spice Traders**, an imagined firm, January 2027. The first entry is a compound entry for the start of the business.
bullets: Purchases return: the supplier is debited, Purchases Return is credited.
Sales return: Sales Return is debited, the customer is credited.
Each side of the journal totals ₹6,15,000.

rows: *(Being business started with cash and furniture)*
*(Being goods purchased on credit from Dhruv Provision Stores)*
*(Being goods sold on credit to Chitra Retail)*
*(Being goods returned to Dhruv Provision Stores)*

visual.alt: Journal of Kolar Spice Traders for January 2027 with seven entries, total 6,15,000 rupees on each side

slides.narration: Kolar Spice Traders starts with cash and furniture, so cash and furniture are debited and capital is credited. Goods bought for cash debit purchases and credit cash. Credit purchases credit the supplier. A sale for cash debits cash and credits sales. A credit sale debits the customer. A return to the supplier debits the supplier and credits purchases return. A return by the customer debits sales return and credits the customer.

slides.heading: Compound entries
slides.body_md: A **compound entry** has more than one account on the debit or the credit side, or both, and its two sides still total the same.

rows: *(Being goods sold, part for cash and the balance on credit)*

visual.alt: Journal table of a compound entry: cash and a debtor debited and sales credited, with equal totals

slides.narration: A compound entry combines several simple entries into one. Here goods are sold, part for cash and the rest on credit. Cash and the customer are both debited, and sales is credited with the total. Do not split the credit between accounts for a single sale. The total of the debits must equal the total of the credits.

slides.heading: Three kinds of discount

rows: A reduction in the list price, given at the time of sale
Not recorded; the net price is entered
Given to a debtor for prompt payment
Obtained from a supplier for prompt payment

visual.alt: Table comparing trade discount, discount allowed and discount received

slides.narration: Trade discount is a reduction in the list price, given at the time of sale. It is not recorded in the books, and the net price is entered. Cash discount allowed is given to a debtor who pays promptly, and is a loss debited to discount allowed. Cash discount received is obtained from a supplier, and is a gain credited to discount received.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: discounts, drawings, a fire and charity
slides.body_md: **Nilgiri Gift House**, an imagined firm, March 2027.
bullets: Discount allowed is debited and discount received is credited.
Goods taken by the owner go to Drawings, credited to Purchases at cost.
Goods destroyed or given away are credited to Purchases.

rows: *(Being cash received from Rajan Menon in full settlement of his account of ₹20,000)*
*(Being cash paid to Salma Khatoon in full settlement of her account of ₹37,500)*
*(Being cash withdrawn by the proprietor for personal use)*
*(Being goods costing ₹6,000 taken by the proprietor for personal use)*

visual.alt: Journal of Nilgiri Gift House for March 2027 with six entries, total 93,000 rupees on each side

slides.narration: Nilgiri Gift House receives cash from a debtor in full settlement, and the shortfall is discount allowed, a debit. It pays a creditor in full settlement, and the saving is discount received, a credit. Cash drawn by the owner is debited to drawings. Goods taken by the owner, destroyed by fire or given as charity are credited to purchases, and the matching debit goes to drawings, loss by fire or charity.

slides.heading: Quick check: the discount entry
slides.body_md: A debtor pays ₹9,400 in full settlement of ₹10,000.
slides.narration: The debtor account is cleared in full, but the firm receives less cash. Decide which account takes the difference, and whether it is a gain or a loss to the firm.

slides.heading: Drawings, losses and charity

rows: Goods destroyed by fire or stolen

visual.alt: Table of four events with the account debited and the account credited: drawings, loss by fire, charity

slides.narration: When the owner withdraws cash, drawings is debited and cash is credited. When the owner takes goods, drawings is debited and purchases is credited, at cost. Goods destroyed by fire or stolen are a loss, so the loss account is debited and purchases is credited. Goods given as charity debit the charity account and credit purchases. No sale is made in any of these cases.

slides.heading: Bad debts, depreciation, interest, outstanding and prepaid items

visual.alt: Table of six items with the account debited and the account credited: bad debts, depreciation, interest, outstanding and prepaid expense

slides.narration: A bad debt is a loss, so bad debts is debited and the debtor is credited. Depreciation is an expense, debited to depreciation and credited to the asset. Interest paid is debited and interest received is credited. An outstanding expense is debited to the expense and credited to a liability account. An expense paid in advance is debited to a prepaid account and credited to the expense.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: bad debt, depreciation, interest and year-end items
slides.body_md: **Palakkad Pottery**, an imagined firm, 31 March 2027.
bullets: A bad debt clears the debtor and records a loss.
Wages outstanding create a liability; insurance paid in advance creates an asset.

rows: *(Being the account of Hari Nair written off as bad)*
*(Being insurance paid in advance for the next year)*

visual.alt: Journal of Palakkad Pottery at 31 March 2027 with six entries, total 26,200 rupees on each side

slides.narration: Palakkad Pottery writes off a debtor, so bad debts is debited and the debtor is credited. Depreciation is debited and machinery is credited. Interest paid is debited with cash credited, and interest received in the bank debits bank and credits interest received. Outstanding wages are debited with a liability credited, and insurance paid in advance is debited as prepaid with the expense credited. Each side totals rupees twenty six thousand two hundred.

slides.heading: The opening entry
slides.body_md: At the start of a year, the balances of the last year are brought forward by one **opening entry**.

rows: Every asset of the firm, each in its own account
Every outside liability, each in its own account
Capital: the balancing figure, assets less liabilities

visual.alt: Table of the opening entry: assets debited, liabilities credited and capital credited as the balancing figure

slides.narration: An opening entry brings the balances of the last year into the new books. Every asset is debited, each in its own account, and every outside liability is credited. Capital is not usually given. It is found as assets less liabilities, and credited as the balancing figure. Debtors and creditors are entered person by person, not as a single total.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: the opening entry of Tiruchi Dairy Mart
slides.body_md: **Tiruchi Dairy Mart**, an imagined firm, 1 April 2026: assets ₹5,95,000, liabilities ₹2,10,000.
bullets: Debtors and creditors are shown person by person.

rows: *(Being assets, liabilities and capital brought forward at the start of the year)*

visual.alt: Opening journal entry of Tiruchi Dairy Mart: assets 5,95,000 debited, liabilities 2,10,000 and capital 3,85,000 credited

slides.narration: Tiruchi Dairy Mart has assets of rupees five lakh ninety five thousand, made up of cash, bank, stock, two debtors, furniture and machinery. It owes rupees two lakh ten thousand to a creditor and a bank. Capital is the balancing figure, assets less liabilities, which is rupees three lakh eighty five thousand. The entry debits each asset and credits each liability and capital, and both sides total rupees five lakh ninety five thousand.

slides.heading: Quick check: the opening entry
slides.body_md: An opening entry debits all assets and credits all liabilities and capital.
slides.narration: Recall which accounts stand on the debit side of an opening entry and which on the credit side. The balancing figure is credited and is the owner claim.

slides.heading: GST: meaning and its three components
slides.body_md: Goods and Services Tax is an **indirect tax** on the supply of goods and services. This is a theory topic only.

rows: A supply within one state, collected by the Centre
State (or union territory) goods and services tax
The same supply, collected by the state
A supply from one state to another, and imports

visual.alt: Table of the three components of GST with their full names and the supplies on which each is charged

slides.narration: Goods and services tax is an indirect tax on the supply of goods and services. Within one state the tax has two parts, central goods and services tax and state goods and services tax, with the union territory tax in a union territory. On a supply from one state to another, integrated goods and services tax is charged. In this course the tax is studied only as theory.

slides.heading: Input tax credit
slides.body_md: Only the **concept** is needed. Journal entries for transactions with GST are not in the ISC Class XI syllabus.

nodes.label: Firm buys inputs and pays tax on them
Firm sells output and collects tax
Tax on inputs is set off against tax on output
Only the difference is paid to the government

visual.alt: Flow of input tax credit: tax paid on inputs is set off against tax collected on output, and only the difference is paid

slides.narration: A registered business pays tax on the inputs it buys and collects tax on what it sells. Input tax credit allows it to set off the first against the second, and pay only the difference. This means tax is paid only on the value the business adds, and tax is not charged on tax at every stage. We study the concept here, and no entries are needed.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2
bullets: The journal is the book of original entry: date, particulars, L.F., debit, credit.
Simple, compound and opening entries, each with a narration.
Discount allowed is a loss; discount received is a gain; trade discount is not recorded.
GST: theory only, with CGST, SGST and IGST and input tax credit.

rows: Book of original entry: date, particulars, L.F., debit and credit
Simple, compound and opening, each with a narration
Allowed is a loss, received is a gain, trade discount is not recorded
Drawings, loss, charity, bad debts, depreciation, interest, outstanding, prepaid
Theory only: CGST, SGST or UTGST, IGST and input tax credit

visual.alt: Summary table of the journal, kinds of entries, discounts, special items and the theory of GST

slides.narration: To sum up. The journal records every transaction first, in date order. Entries may be simple, compound or opening, and each has a narration. Drawings, losses, charity, bad debts, depreciation, interest, outstanding and prepaid items follow their own rules. Goods and services tax is a theoretical topic with three components, and input tax credit lets a business pay tax only on the value it adds.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write the debit first and the credit after To, with a narration.
Credit Purchases, not Sales, for goods taken, lost or given away.
Work out each discount before writing the entry.

rows: Write the debit first and indent the credit after "To"
The standard form earns the presentation mark
Add a narration to every entry
Narration is expected and carries a mark
Credit Purchases for goods that leave the stock unsold
A common slip is to use Sales
Check that debit and credit totals agree

visual.alt: Exam tips table for the journal

slides.narration: In the examination, write the debit first and indent the credit after the word To, and add a narration to every entry. Credit purchases, not sales, for goods taken by the owner, lost or given away. Work out discounts and the capital in an opening entry before writing the entry, and check that the two sides of each entry agree.

notes.title: Accounting Equation and Journal — Notes

sections.heading: 1. The accounting equation
sections.body_md:
A firm owns resources, its **assets**, and every asset is financed either by outsiders, the **liabilities**, or by the owner, the **capital**. So the resources always match the claims on them:

**Assets = Liabilities + Capital**

The equation holds after every transaction because each transaction has two aspects of equal value. Rearranged, it finds the capital (assets less liabilities) or the outside liabilities (assets less capital) when two of the three are known.

**Uses:** it tests that the books are in balance, finds a missing element, and shows the effect of a transaction. **Limit:** it covers only what can be stated in money and it does not show sales or profit by itself.

key_terms.definition_md: Assets = Liabilities + Capital; the resources of a firm equal the claims against them.
Resources owned by the firm that have value, such as cash, stock, debtors and machinery.
Amounts owed by the firm to outsiders, such as creditors and a bank loan.
The owner's claim: investment plus profit left in, less drawings.

rows: Checks the position after a transaction

visual.alt: Table of the three forms of the accounting equation and what each finds

sections.heading: 2. Effect of transactions on the equation

key_terms.definition_md: Cash or goods taken by the owner for personal use; they reduce capital.
Closing capital less opening capital, plus drawings, less fresh capital.

Sold goods costing ₹12,000 on credit for ₹14,500

sections.heading: 3. Double entry and the classification of accounts
sections.body_md:
Under the **double entry system** every transaction affects two aspects, one debited and one credited, for equal amounts. So the total debits equal the total credits.

**Traditional classification:** personal accounts (natural, artificial, representative), real accounts (tangible, intangible) and nominal accounts.

**Modern classification:** assets, liabilities, capital, revenues (incomes) and expenses (losses).

Book texts differ on a few accounts (for example the bank account, and Purchases and Sales); in every case the side to debit or credit is the same, so use the rule of the modern class when in doubt.

sections.heading: 4. Rules of debit and credit
sections.body_md:
**Traditional rules**

- Personal: debit the receiver, credit the giver.
- Real: debit what comes in, credit what goes out.
- Nominal: debit all expenses and losses, credit all incomes and gains.

**Modern rules:** an asset or an expense is increased by a debit; a liability, capital or revenue is increased by a credit; the opposite side is used for a decrease. The **Drawings account** is debited because drawings reduce the capital.

Both methods always give the same entry: for example, machinery bought for cash debits the machinery and credits cash.

sections.heading: 5. The journal: meaning, advantages and format
sections.body_md:
The **journal** is the book of original entry: each transaction is recorded in it first, in date order, with the accounts debited and credited and a **narration**. From it the entries are posted to the ledger (the next chapter).

**Advantages:** a record in date order, both aspects of a transaction together, a narration for reference, fewer errors, and evidence for checking.

**Format:** five columns, namely date, particulars, ledger folio (L.F.), debit amount and credit amount. The account to be debited is written first with Dr.; the account to be credited follows on the next line, indented, after the word To; the narration, beginning with Being, is written below.

sections.heading: 6. Journal entries: simple, compound, opening and special items
sections.body_md:
A **simple entry** has one debit and one credit. A **compound entry** has several accounts on one side or both, with equal totals. The **opening entry** debits every asset and credits every liability; capital, the balancing figure (assets less liabilities), is credited.

**Discounts:** trade discount is not recorded; discount allowed (to debtors) is a loss and is debited; discount received (from creditors) is a gain and is credited.

**Special items:** drawings (cash: credit Cash; goods: credit Purchases); goods lost by fire or theft, or given as charity (debit the loss or Charity, credit Purchases); bad debts (debit Bad Debts, credit the debtor); depreciation (debit Depreciation, credit the asset); interest paid (debit) and received (credit); outstanding expense (credit a liability account); prepaid expense (debit an asset account).

sections.heading: 7. Goods and Services Tax (GST): a brief theory
sections.body_md:
**GST** is an indirect tax on the supply of goods and services. It has three components: **CGST** and **SGST** (**UTGST** in a union territory) are charged together on a supply within one state or union territory, and **IGST** on a supply from one state to another.

**Input tax credit** lets a registered business set off the tax paid on its inputs against the tax payable on its output, so that tax is paid only on the value added.

This chapter treats GST as theory only: rates, computations and journal entries for transactions with GST are not part of the ISC Class XI syllabus.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** ₹3,50,000. Capital is assets less liabilities, 4,80,000 − 1,30,000 = 3,50,000. ₹6,10,000 adds the two figures, ₹1,30,000 is only the liabilities and ₹4,80,000 is the assets before the outside claims are deducted.

assets fall by ₹18,000 and liabilities fall by ₹18,000
assets rise by ₹18,000 and liabilities rise by ₹18,000

questions.stem_md: Give any two uses of the accounting equation in an imagined business, and one limitation of it.
questions.solution_md: Two uses at one mark each and a limitation for the third mark.

questions.stem_md: A class studies indirect taxes using an imagined bakery in Pune as its example. Goods and Services Tax is best described as

options.text_md: an indirect tax on the supply of goods and services, charged at each stage with credit for the tax already paid
a direct tax on the income of the owner of a business
a tax levied only on goods imported into the country
a fee paid once, when a firm is registered

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** an indirect tax on the supply of goods and services, charged at each stage with credit for the tax already paid. It is a single indirect tax on supplies of goods and services, with a credit at each stage for tax paid earlier. A tax on income is a direct tax, it is not confined to imports, and it is not a one-time registration fee.

questions.stem_md: A registered firm in Pune, imagined for this question, sells goods to a buyer in Chennai, which is in another state. The tax charged on this supply is

options.text_md: central and state goods and services tax together
state goods and services tax alone
integrated goods and services tax, collected by the Centre
union territory goods and services tax alone

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** integrated goods and services tax, collected by the Centre. A supply from one state to another is taxed as integrated goods and services tax. The central and state taxes together apply to a supply inside one state, and the union territory tax to a supply inside a union territory.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Input tax credit lets a registered firm in an imagined town set off the tax it paid on its purchases against the tax it owes on its sales.

**Reason (R):** Input tax credit is a cash refund that the government pays to every buyer at the end of the year.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The credit is a set-off against tax payable, so the firm pays tax only on the value it adds. It is not a refund paid to every buyer, so R is false.

questions.stem_md: A registered firm in Jaipur, imagined for this question, sells goods to a customer in Jaipur itself. The tax on this supply has two parts: central goods and services tax and state goods and services tax.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** A supply within one state is taxed by the Centre and the state, as CGST and SGST.

questions.stem_md: On a sale within its own state, an imagined firm charges central goods and services tax and ___ goods and services tax; on a sale to another state it charges ___ goods and services tax.
questions.solution_md: Within a state the two parts are central and state; between states the single tax is integrated goods and services tax.

questions.stem_md: Name the three components of Goods and Services Tax and state the kind of supply on which each is charged.
questions.solution_md: One mark for the pair charged inside a state and one for the tax charged between states.

answer.model_answer_md:
**CGST** (central) and **SGST** (state; **UTGST** in a union territory) are charged together on a supply made within one state or union territory.

**IGST** (integrated) is charged on a supply from one state to another, and on imports.

IGST on a supply between states

questions.stem_md: Explain input tax credit under Goods and Services Tax, using an imagined firm that buys raw material and sells finished goods. No amounts are needed.
questions.solution_md: Define the credit, show the set-off in a business, and state why it helps.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Meaning:** a registered business may deduct the tax it paid on the inputs it bought for its business from the tax it has to pay on what it sells.

**Example:** a firm making cane baskets pays tax when it buys cane and, later, collects tax when it sells the baskets. It sets the first against the second and deposits only the difference.

**Benefit:** tax is paid only on the value the firm adds, so tax is not charged again on tax at every stage.
